sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Give the first read a purpose: learn enough structure to locate evidence efficiently. After reading a question, name the task before examining its choices. Is it asking for an explicit detail, an inference, a word’s local meaning, a paragraph’s function, or a relationship between sources? Different tasks require different evidence. A detail usually sends you back to a narrow location; a summary needs the passage’s controlling movement. Rereading the entire passage for every question hides this difference and consumes time without guaranteeing a better decision.

If two choices remain, compare them against the same piece of evidence. Ask which word in each choice creates the disagreement. The decisive difference is often scope, certainty, chronology, speaker, or purpose rather than an unfamiliar vocabulary word. A choice saying every participant is not interchangeable with one saying the interviewed group. Identify the mismatch in a short phrase. If you cannot locate support after a deliberate attempt, select the best available answer, flag it, and move. Use a later return to test one unresolved issue rather than restart the question from nothing.

At each passage transition, check elapsed time and unanswered items. Reserving a brief final review is useful only if you have selected answers throughout the section. This practice lab records raw accuracy on original material; it cannot promise a particular ACT scaled score. Your score goal should guide careful review of repeated errors, not encourage claims that a small practice set predicts a thirty-six. Build speed from a consistent evidence process, then examine whether timing or comprehension changes when you use complete forty-minute forms.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: Before revealing an explanation, record a specific confidence judgment. Afterward, compare your chosen answer with the actual evidence rather than simply reading why the key is correct. Write the smallest rule that would have changed your decision: return to the stated date, separate the quoted speaker from the author, reject a claim about every resident, or compare proportions using the same denominator. A note such as read more carefully is too broad to guide another attempt. Name the exact decision you made and the evidence you overlooked.

Use the error-cause control to distinguish content or comprehension gaps from timing, a misread stem, a rushed choice, or uncertainty between two options. A slow correct answer can still reveal a weak process, while a quick wrong answer can reveal unjustified confidence. Review at least one tempting distractor and explain its defect using the passage. If the explanation sounds equally applicable to every wrong choice, make it more concrete. The point is to acquire a transferable check, not memorize which letter happened to be right in one question.

After the repair, do a fresh set rather than immediately repeating the same remembered item. Keep full-section questions separate from topic drills so the timed result measures a new decision. This lab saves completed practice to your signed-in account and shows mastery only after sufficient distinct-question evidence. A topic badge is a signal about this bank, not proof of an official scaled score. When today’s plan exceeds the available budget, unfinished tasks remain visible and carry forward in order; extra work should be a deliberate choice rather than an invisible doubling of tomorrow’s assignment.

passage.title: The Second Entrance
passage.context:
After his father’s injury, Luis began entering their apartment building through the side door, which had no steps. The route took longer. At first he described it as the inconvenient entrance and hurried his father along it whenever the weather threatened rain.

One afternoon they passed a neighbor tending the narrow garden beside the path. Luis had lived in the building for five years without learning her name. His father stopped to ask about the beans. During later walks they noticed which plants leaned toward the fence and which survived the shade. The neighbor saved a cutting for their kitchen window.

When his father recovered, Luis used the front steps again for quick errands. But he sometimes chose the side path alone. It had not become shorter, and the front entrance had not become less useful. The route he had called inconvenient now held encounters he would otherwise have missed. He stopped referring to the doors as the usual entrance and the other one.

how changing observation times can revise a planning conclusion
why climbing structures should never be maintained
that preschool children do not use playgrounds

passage.title: Who Uses the Playground?
passage.context:
A planning office studied playground use on four weekday mornings. Its observers counted many preschool children and few teenagers. A draft report recommended removing a climbing structure designed for older children because it appeared rarely used.

Before the recommendation was finalized, a librarian asked whether observations had occurred after school. They had not. The office added afternoon and Saturday sessions. Those visits recorded older children using the structure, although morning use remained low.

The final report separated use by time period. It no longer treated a quiet structure during preschool hours as evidence of little use overall. The office retained the structure and scheduled maintenance when both morning and afternoon use were typically lowest. The revised study still covered only selected weeks; its authors recommended revisiting the pattern when the school calendar changed.

lesson.title: Algebra
lesson.intro: Make algebra automatic while keeping every restriction and sign. Write the one step most likely to go wrong; then verify the candidate in the original statement.

sections.heading: Quadratics and inequalities
body: Factor when the numbers cooperate. Otherwise use the quadratic formula or complete the square. In an inequality, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign.

Worked example: x² − 8x + 15 = (x − 3)(x − 5), so its zeros are 3 and 5. The product is negative between the zeros and positive outside. Thus x² − 8x + 15 < 0 has 3 < x < 5; strict inequalities exclude the zeros.
sections.tip: Test a point from each interval when the expression’s sign is uncertain.

examples.label: Cross-term check
examples.text: (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y². Never drop the 2xy term.

sections.heading: Recognize polynomial structure before calculating
body: Look for a common factor, a difference of squares, a perfect-square trinomial, or a pair of grouped terms with the same factor. A cubic does not automatically require a long computation. Factoring reveals all the zeros at once and preserves repeated roots. If the question asks only for a roots’ sum or product, use the coefficient relationships instead of solving each root.

Worked example: p(x) = x³ + 2x² − 9x − 18 groups as x²(x + 2) − 9(x + 2). Therefore p(x) = (x + 2)(x − 3)(x + 3), with zeros −2, 3, −3. Their sum is −2. For 5x² − 15x + 2, the roots’ sum is 15/5 = 3 and their product is 2/5 even though the individual roots are awkward.

A provided zero can also determine an unknown coefficient: substitute that input and set the output to zero. To recover a polynomial from two zeros r and s, start with a(x − r)(x − s); use a supplied point to find a. Do not assume a = 1. Division by x − r leaves remainder p(r), so a remainder question often needs one substitution rather than long division.

lesson.title: Algebra
lesson.intro: Make algebra automatic while keeping every restriction and sign. Write the one step most likely to go wrong; then verify the candidate in the original statement.

sections.heading: Parameters, identities, and exponent equations
body: A parameter is a fixed but unknown number. Decide what behavior the prompt requires: one solution, no solutions, infinitely many solutions, or a repeated quadratic root. For Ax = B, nonzero A gives one solution; A = 0 with B ≠ 0 gives none; A = B = 0 gives infinitely many. In a polynomial identity, match corresponding coefficients because equality must hold for every input.

Worked example: (k − 3)x = 0 has infinitely many solutions when k = 3, because both sides become zero for every x. In x² + 8x + c = 0, exactly one real root requires discriminant 8² − 4c = 0, giving c = 16. For a(x + 2)² + b = ax² + 12x + 7, matching the linear coefficient gives 4a = 12, so a = 3 and then b = −5.

For exponent equations, rewrite both sides with the same base when possible. A product of powers adds exponents, while a power raised to another power multiplies them. For example, 3^(2x − 1) = 81 = 3⁴ gives 2x − 1 = 4 and x = 5/2. Keep the whole exponent in parentheses and avoid treating an exponent as a multiplication factor.
sections.tip: For a quadratic, discriminant positive means two real roots, zero means one, and negative means none.

examples.label: Worked example

sections.heading: Fast methods and an algebra error log
body: Back-solving answer choices is useful when the question seeks a single number and direct algebra looks long. Start with a middle-sized choice if the relationship is monotonic, then use whether the result is too large or too small to narrow the rest. For an identity or equivalent expression, plug in simple allowed values to eliminate choices, but remember that agreement at one input does not prove an identity.

Worked example: to compare proposed forms of (2x + 1)(x − 3), x = 0 checks the constant −3 and x = 1 checks the output −6. Those tests quickly reject many incorrect signs, after which expanding gives 2x² − 5x − 3 as a proof. Avoid x values that make all choices equal, such as zero when every choice contains a factor of x.

In timed work, write a brief line showing the risky step: a negative division, a distribution over subtraction, or a denominator restriction. If no clear route appears after a short attempt, mark the problem and return after securing clearer points. After each drill, label an error as concept, setup, arithmetic, restriction, or requested quantity. Redo the problem without viewing the explanation; recognizing the explanation is not the same as reproducing the method.

body: Factor when the numbers cooperate. Otherwise use the quadratic formula or complete the square. In an inequality, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign.

sections.heading: Combine information only after matching conditions
body: At a confluence, Stream A supplies 30 L/s at 4 mg/L and B supplies 10 L/s at 12 mg/L. Their pollutant mass flows are 120 mg/s each. Mixing gives 240 mg/s in 40 L/s, or 6 mg/L. The simple average of 4 and 12 is 8, but it wrongly treats the incoming water amounts as equal. A weighted average follows the physical contributions and matches the measured outgoing concentration.

Across multiple studies, identify settings that genuinely match before transferring a value. Equal row position is not evidence of equal treatments. A table might sort one study by light and another by nitrate, so the third row can represent different combinations. Match species, time, temperature, concentration, and other relevant labels. If two plots use different units for the same variable, convert before comparison. Milligrams and grams differ by a factor of 1,000, even if their numbers look similar.

examples.label: Weight by water flow
examples.text: Incoming pollutant = 30×4 + 10×12 = 240 mg/s. Incoming water = 40 L/s. Mixed concentration = 240/40 = 6 mg/L, not the unweighted 8 mg/L.

evidence.title: Two streams merge
evidence.context: Stream A and Stream B join to form C. Samples were taken simultaneously during steady flow. Assume the pollutant is dissolved, conserved during mixing, and evenly mixed in C. Pollutant mass flow in g/s equals concentration in mg/L multiplied by water flow in L/s, divided by 1,000.

sections.heading: Audit a choice quickly and record the actual error
body: Before submitting an answer, perform a short evidence check: the requested row, the correct column or series, the right unit, and the appropriate denominator. Then make sure the resulting number answers the question’s wording. An arithmetic answer can be internally correct but belong to a different quantity. For Cup B, 1.5°C is the temperature increase; 21.5°C is the final temperature after adding the 20°C start. Both are sensible numbers, so wording is decisive.

During review, identify whether a missed item came from locating evidence, calculating, or interpreting the request. Recompute one item of the same type without seeing the answer. If you chose an insect count when density was requested, practice a new unequal-area comparison. If you chose a germination percentage when root length was requested, practice locating the exact labeled column. A specific corrected habit is more useful than simply rereading that the answer was wrong.

lesson.title: Semicolons, Colons, Dashes & Apostrophes
lesson.intro: Semicolons, colons, dashes, and apostrophes show up on every ACT English section, a steady handful of questions per test beyond the comma items. The rules are mechanical: each mark is either legal in a spot or it isn't. Label each side of the mark as a complete clause or a fragment, and the right answer follows.

sections.heading: Semicolons join two independent clauses
body: A semicolon does one main job on the ACT: it links two independent clauses, each of which could stand alone as a sentence. Read each side. If both sides could end with a period, a semicolon is legal.

A handy shortcut: a semicolon works in exactly the same spots a period would. If you can swap in a period without creating a fragment, the semicolon is correct. If either side is a fragment, the semicolon is wrong.

One exception to that shortcut: a semicolon replaces a coordinating conjunction, so it never sits next to one. A period before 'But' or 'And' can be legal style, but '; but' and '; and' are always wrong on the ACT. When a FANBOYS word joins the clauses, a comma goes before it, not a semicolon.

Semicolons have one rare second job: separating list items that already contain commas, as in 'We visited Austin, Texas; Tulsa, Oklahoma; and Boise, Idaho.' If the items carry internal commas, those semicolons are legal even though no full clause is in sight.

examples.text: The lab closed early; the storm knocked out the power.
examples.label: Two independent clauses

examples.text: The lab closed early; because of the storm.
examples.label: Second part is a fragment

sections.tip: Period test: if a period works there, so does the semicolon. One exception: never put a semicolon next to a FANBOYS conjunction. '; but' is always wrong; use ', but' instead.

sections.heading: Colons introduce after a complete clause
body: A colon announces that something follows: a list, an explanation, or a single word. The catch the ACT tests over and over is that the words before the colon must form a complete sentence.
What comes after the colon does not need to be a complete sentence. That is the key difference from a semicolon, which demands a full clause on both sides.
The ACT's favorite colon trap splits a verb or a preposition from what follows. A colon after 'such as' or 'including' is wrong every time, because the words before the colon cannot stand alone.

examples.text: She packed one thing: courage.
examples.label: Complete clause, then a colon

lesson.title: Semicolons, Colons, Dashes & Apostrophes
lesson.intro: Semicolons, colons, dashes, and apostrophes show up on every ACT English section, a steady handful of questions per test beyond the comma items. The rules are mechanical: each mark is either legal in a spot or it isn't. Label each side of the mark as a complete clause or a fragment, and the right answer follows.

sections.heading: Apostrophes: possession vs. contraction
body: Apostrophes mark possession or stand in for missing letters. For a singular noun, add 's (the dog's leash). For a plural noun already ending in s, add only an apostrophe (the dogs' leashes).

The traps live in the pronouns. 'Its' is possessive and takes no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is.' 'Whose' is possessive; 'who's' means 'who is.' 'Their' is possessive; 'they're' means 'they are.' A noun that is just plural, with no ownership, gets no apostrophe at all.

examples.text: The committee published its report; the senators' votes were unanimous.
examples.label: Possessive 'its' takes no apostrophe; plural possessive adds one after the s

examples.text: The committee published it's report.
examples.label: 'It's' means 'it is,' which fails here

sections.tip: Expand the contraction. If 'it is' or 'who is' makes sense, use the apostrophe; if not, use the possessive.

sections.heading: Quotation marks and surrounding punctuation
body: On the ACT, periods and commas go inside the closing quotation mark. This is the American convention the test enforces every time.

When a quotation is introduced by a full clause, a colon can lead into it; when it is woven into the sentence with a verb like 'said,' a comma does the work. Match the punctuation to how the quote is attached.

examples.text: "Wait here," she said.
examples.label: Comma inside the quotation mark

examples.text: "Wait here", she said.
examples.label: Comma outside the mark; the ACT puts it inside

sections.tip: Periods and commas always tuck inside the closing quote.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Read the answer choices first. When the words barely change and the marks do (a comma, semicolon, colon, and dash shuffled across four choices), you are in a punctuation question, and clause structure decides it.

Step 1: find the boundary the underline sits on. Step 2: label each side as a complete clause or a fragment. Both sides complete: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction can join them. Complete clause followed by a fragment that explains it: a colon or a single dash. A fragment on either side of a semicolon kills that choice.

Apostrophe questions look different: the choices shuffle its/it's or whose/who's, or slide an apostrophe around an s. Expand the contraction in your head and check whether the sentence still makes sense.
sections.tip: Two choices that do the same grammatical job (a colon and a single dash, or a period and a semicolon) cancel each other out: the answer is one of the others.

The rules are mechanical: each mark is either legal in a spot or it isn't. Label each side of the mark as a complete clause or a fragment, and the right answer follows.

sections.heading: Semicolons join two independent clauses
body: A semicolon does one main job on the ACT: it links two independent clauses, each of which could stand alone as a sentence. Read each side. If both sides could end with a period, a semicolon is legal.

A handy shortcut: a semicolon works in exactly the same spots a period would. If you can swap in a period without creating a fragment, the semicolon is correct. If either side is a fragment, the semicolon is wrong.

One exception to that shortcut: a semicolon replaces a coordinating conjunction, so it never sits next to one. A period before 'But' or 'And' can be legal style, but '; but' and '; and' are always wrong on the ACT. When a FANBOYS word joins the clauses, a comma goes before it, not a semicolon.

Semicolons have one rare second job: separating list items that already contain commas, as in 'We visited Austin, Texas; Tulsa, Oklahoma; and Boise, Idaho.' If the items carry internal commas, those semicolons are legal even though no full clause is in sight.

examples.text: The lab closed early; the storm knocked out the power.
examples.label: Two independent clauses

examples.text: The lab closed early; because of the storm.
examples.label: Second part is a fragment

sections.tip: Period test: if a period works there, so does the semicolon. One exception: never put a semicolon next to a FANBOYS conjunction. '; but' is always wrong; use ', but' instead.

sections.heading: Colons introduce after a complete clause
body: A colon announces that something follows: a list, an explanation, or a single word. The catch the ACT tests over and over is that the words before the colon must form a complete sentence.
What comes after the colon does not need to be a complete sentence. That is the key difference from a semicolon, which demands a full clause on both sides.
The ACT's favorite colon trap splits a verb or a preposition from what follows. A colon after 'such as' or 'including' is wrong every time, because the words before the colon cannot stand alone.

lesson.title: Details, sequence, and cause
lesson.intro: Locate exact evidence and distinguish a sequence from a causal explanation. Learn the evidence process, study six worked examples, and test it on three new passages.

sections.heading: Separate sequence from cause
body: An event occurring after another event does not automatically mean the first caused the second. Detail questions sometimes ask for the order of events, while other questions ask for a cause explicitly supplied by the passage. Keep those tasks separate. In a pilot that adds an evening return window and reminder messages at the same time, improved returns follow both changes. The passage can report that sequence without assigning the entire improvement to either change alone.

Build a quick sequence when dates or stages matter: initial expectation, trial, observation, revised report, further test. Then examine causal language. Because, led to, and attributed to can establish a stated explanation; coincided with marks a weaker relationship. A choice may preserve the right events but reverse their order or strengthen coincidence into proof. When the stem asks according to the passage, report the text’s claim faithfully even if you personally think another explanation is likely. Your outside knowledge cannot supply a causal statement the writer did not make.

examples.text:
Passage A — Theater director
Our theater’s facade is intact, but the stage rigging is unsafe. Preserving the room exactly as it stood in 1930 would make it impossible to use. I want to retain the painted ceiling and the worn foyer steps while replacing the cables above the stage. A public building survives through repeated encounters. A locked theater is a photograph of itself.

Passage B — Architectural historian
Use can help preserve a theater, but “modernization” is sometimes a generous word for erasure. The original stage equipment reveals how productions were mounted; removing all of it would sever that record. I support new safety systems, provided representative old mechanisms remain visible and the alterations are documented. Preservation need not mean freezing a building. It means knowing what changes cost.

Both writers are responding to a proposed renovation. Neither disputes that the existing rigging is unsafe. The debate concerns how to change the theater while retaining what makes its past legible.

Question: Which feature does the director specifically want to retain?

Supported answer: the painted ceiling

Reason: Passage A pairs retaining the painted ceiling with replacing unsafe cables. The supported answer is “the painted ceiling.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 2: Two Ways to Keep a Theater

sections.heading: Control the unit, speaker, and condition
body: A detail’s unit is part of the fact. A tool-return count measures tools, not borrowers. Occupied seats at two times do not count distinct visitors over the whole afternoon. A map assembled from volunteer participants reflects that group, not automatically every resident. Before accepting a number or comparison, identify what is counted, over which period, and under what conditions. These qualifiers often do more work than the number itself.

Also track speakers. A visitor may propose a strong interpretation that the researchers immediately qualify; the passage does not thereby endorse the visitor’s claim. A director and a historian can agree about unsafe rigging while disagreeing about retained machinery. When an option says the report, the historian, or the narrator believes something, check that speaker specifically. An accurate sentence from Passage A is not necessarily an accurate description of Passage B. Underline the attribution mentally and reread the sentence where the opinion appears.

examples.text:
A town introduced a Saturday bus between the library and three neighborhoods. Before the pilot, residents at public meetings had asked for daily service. The transport office could initially fund only eight Saturdays. It counted riders and invited anonymous comments after each trip.

The first Saturday drew twelve passengers. By the eighth, twenty-nine people rode. Several comments praised the library stop; others asked for an earlier departure. One resident wrote that the trip was useful but too infrequent for a weekday job. A council member called the growing attendance encouraging. The office’s report used a more guarded phrase: the figures supported continuing the trial, not yet expanding it to every day.

The report noted two limits. The trial took place during a summer reading program, and it did not measure how many riders would pay a fare. The office proposed another eight weeks after the program ended, with an optional fare question on the comment card. The council approved the additional trial without promising a permanent route.

Question: Why does the report mention the summer reading program?

Supported answer: It may have affected demand during the pilot

Reason: The program is listed as a limit on how confidently summer ridership can predict later demand. The supported answer is “It may have affected demand during the pilot.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 3: The Bus Pilot

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: Why did “Good morning” initially seem inadequate?
choices: The original character never spoke to strangers
The character also used the source greeting at night
The editor wanted every greeting removed
questions.explanation: The nighttime uses show that the source phrase is not limited to the time meaning of the first English choice. The supported answer is “The character also used the source greeting at night.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: A Translator’s Margins
passage.context:
The translator’s first draft rendered a character’s repeated greeting as “Good morning.” It was smooth English, but the editor noticed that the character used the greeting at night as well. In the source language the phrase had an everyday social meaning that was not limited to time of day.

The translator considered replacing it with “Hello.” That would remove the odd nighttime mornings, but it would also remove a small difference in how the character addressed familiar people and strangers. She reviewed each occurrence, noting who spoke and who answered. Eventually she chose two English expressions depending on the relationship, then added a short note explaining the source phrase’s range.

An early reader complained that the note broke the story’s flow. Another said it helped make sense of a later conversation. The translator trimmed the note but kept it. She did not claim that the new version reproduced every association of the original. Her goal was to preserve the greeting’s work within this particular story, while making the unavoidable tradeoff visible.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: What did the owner want to do with his ledger?
choices: leave it for another visitor facing the same problem
sell it to recover the lamp’s purchase price
use it to prove that no repairs had occurred
return it to the café’s supplier
questions.explanation: He explicitly wants to leave the copied tests for the next visitor with the same problem. The supported answer is “leave it for another visitor facing the same problem.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Returning the Ledger
passage.context:
At a repair café, volunteers taught visitors how to mend small household objects. The coordinator originally reported success by counting completed repairs. After a month she discovered that a visitor had returned three times with the same lamp. The volunteer who worked with him had repaired the switch on the first visit, shown him how to test a cord on the second, and helped him diagnose a loose connection on the third.

The coordinator worried that the repeat visits inflated the total. The volunteer agreed that the chart needed clearer labels but argued that the repeated work had another value: the visitor now understood how the lamp functioned. The café began recording both completed repairs and teaching sessions, explaining that the figures could overlap.

At the next meeting the lamp’s owner brought back a small ledger in which he had copied the tests he learned. He wanted to leave it for the next visitor with the same problem. The coordinator placed it near the repair tools. The lamp appeared only once on the new list of repaired objects, but its lessons had already traveled farther.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: Why does the team recommend another round of observations?
choices: The residents refused to be interviewed
The street corner moved to another neighborhood
Nearby construction temporarily changed vehicle routes
questions.explanation: The final paragraph identifies the temporary route change as a reason to repeat the observations. The supported answer is “Nearby construction temporarily changed vehicle routes.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Measuring a Quiet Street
passage.context:
Residents said that a traffic change made their street quieter. A student team measured sound at the same corner before and after the change, at three fixed times of day. The average reading fell at two times and rose slightly at the third. The team also counted heavy vehicles and interviewed residents.

The interviews described fewer sudden truck noises, even when the overall reading was similar. One resident said a steady hum was easier to ignore than an unexpected engine roar. The team’s report separated average sound level from the frequency of disruptive peaks. It did not treat either measure as a complete description of how people experienced the street.

Because construction on a nearby road temporarily altered vehicle routes, the team recommended repeating the observations after construction ended. It reported the initial changes and the residents’ comments, but avoided attributing every change to the new traffic rule. The street’s experience could improve in a way an average alone missed, while the cause of that improvement still required investigation.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: What does Jae leave in the case?
choices: a new bridge for the teacher
a note about softly started notes
questions.explanation: The final paragraph specifies the note and where he puts it. The supported answer is “a note about softly started notes.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: The Borrowed Violin
passage.context:
When Jae borrowed the school’s oldest violin, he expected a temporary instrument until his repaired one returned. The old case smelled faintly of cedar. A faded label inside listed six former borrowers. During rehearsal he kept checking the tuning, irritated by a bridge that seemed unfamiliar under his hand.

His teacher asked him to play one phrase slowly rather than testing the violin with scales. He noticed that a softly started note carried farther than he expected. He still missed the easy response of his own instrument, but he stopped treating each difference as a defect. At the end of the week he played the borrowed violin at a small recital.

When his own violin came back, Jae returned the school instrument with a note describing the softly started notes. He put the note beneath the list of names. It was not a recommendation that everyone should prefer the old violin. It was something the next borrower might try before deciding what the instrument could do.

questions.subject: reading
questions.questionText: What did the curator shorten?
choices: a technical description of the weave
questions.explanation: The final paragraph identifies the weave description as the material she shortened. The supported answer is “a technical description of the weave.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: The Museum Label
passage.context:
A museum’s label described a woven basket as a storage vessel. During a community consultation, a maker explained that baskets of this type were also exchanged when families helped one another during harvest. Its value involved relationships as well as its capacity to hold grain.

The curator did not remove the storage description. It was accurate, but incomplete. She added a paragraph about exchange, named the consultation, and asked permission to quote the maker’s account. The revised label kept the object’s material and date at the top and placed the new account directly below them.

Some visitors read only the first lines. The curator therefore shortened a technical description of the weave and moved the exchange information higher. She wanted visitors to see function and relationship together, without presenting one person’s account as the complete history of every basket. Future labels would include additional voices when available.

units.title: Check a paraphrase without demanding identical wording

lesson.title: Details, sequence, and cause
lesson.intro: Locate exact evidence and distinguish a sequence from a causal explanation. Learn the evidence process, study six worked examples, and test it on three new passages.

sections.heading: Check a paraphrase without demanding identical wording
body: The right answer may translate a stated phrase into simpler language. A report’s guarded wording can mean that evidence supports continuing a trial without justifying daily expansion. The passage need not use the exact word cautious for that paraphrase to be correct. Match the relationship and strength of the claim, not merely repeated vocabulary. Conversely, an option can borrow several words from the passage and connect them in a way the text never does.

After finding the evidence, compare each option’s actor, action, object, and qualifier. A choice saying the curator changes the caption is supported; one saying she removes the first map reverses the preserved-project detail. Reject an option for a concrete mismatch rather than for sounding unfamiliar. If the fact appears in two places, use both when necessary to resolve a pronoun or chronology. This evidence-first habit makes explicit-detail questions efficient while preventing careless substitutions that can be costly near the top of the score range.

examples.text:
Nico spent the first morning of the sound workshop recording traffic. The instructor asked him to choose a location and listen there for ten minutes before touching the recorder. He picked the bridge because he knew what he would hear: engines, tires, horns. He pressed the recording button after less than a minute.

When the instructor played his clip, the traffic filled every second. “You found what you expected,” she said. She sent him back without suggesting a different location. This time Nico stayed under the bridge. He noticed water striking a loose piece of timber, a bicycle chain clicking above him, and pauses in which the river seemed louder than the road. He began recording only after the ten minutes had passed.

That afternoon he compared the clips. The second still contained engines; listening had not removed them. But it also held the soft intervals he had missed. He labeled the first file “Bridge” and hesitated over the second. Finally he gave both files the same name and added only the dates. The place had not changed enough to explain the difference.

Question: What instruction does Nico initially fail to follow?

Supported answer: listening for ten minutes before recording

Reason: He presses the button after less than a minute despite the explicit ten-minute instruction. The supported answer is “listening for ten minutes before recording.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 4: Listening Beneath the Bridge

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Give the first read a purpose: learn enough structure to locate evidence efficiently. After reading a question, name the task before examining its choices. Is it asking for an explicit detail, an inference, a word’s local meaning, a paragraph’s function, or a relationship between sources? Different tasks require different evidence. A detail usually sends you back to a narrow location; a summary needs the passage’s controlling movement. Rereading the entire passage for every question hides this difference and consumes time without guaranteeing a better decision.

If two choices remain, compare them against the same piece of evidence. Ask which word in each choice creates the disagreement. The decisive difference is often scope, certainty, chronology, speaker, or purpose rather than an unfamiliar vocabulary word. A choice saying every participant is not interchangeable with one saying the interviewed group. Identify the mismatch in a short phrase. If you cannot locate support after a deliberate attempt, select the best available answer, flag it, and move. Use a later return to test one unresolved issue rather than restart the question from nothing.

At each passage transition, check elapsed time and unanswered items. Reserving a brief final review is useful only if you have selected answers throughout the section. This practice lab records raw accuracy on original material; it cannot promise a particular ACT scaled score. Your score goal should guide careful review of repeated errors, not encourage claims that a small practice set predicts a thirty-six. sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: Before revealing an explanation, record a specific confidence judgment. Afterward, compare your chosen answer with the actual evidence rather than simply reading why the key is correct. lesson.title: Details, sequence, and cause
lesson.intro: Locate exact evidence and distinguish a sequence from a causal explanation. Learn the evidence process, study six worked examples, and test it on three new passages.

sections.heading: Separate sequence from cause
body: An event occurring after another event does not automatically mean the first caused the second. Detail questions sometimes ask for the order of events, while other questions ask for a cause explicitly supplied by the passage. Keep those tasks separate. In a pilot that adds an evening return window and reminder messages at the same time, improved returns follow both changes. The passage can report that sequence without assigning the entire improvement to either change alone.

Build a quick sequence when dates or stages matter: initial expectation, trial, observation, revised report, further test. Then examine causal language. Because, led to, and attributed to can establish a stated explanation; coincided with marks a weaker relationship. A choice may preserve the right events but reverse their order or strengthen coincidence into proof. When the stem asks according to the passage, report the text’s claim faithfully even if you personally think another explanation is likely. Your outside knowledge cannot supply a causal statement the writer did not make.

examples.text:
Passage A — Theater director
Our theater’s facade is intact, but the stage rigging is unsafe. Preserving the room exactly as it stood in 1930 would make it impossible to use. I want to retain the painted ceiling and the worn foyer steps while replacing the cables above the stage. A public building survives through repeated encounters. A locked theater is a photograph of itself.

Passage B — Architectural historian
Use can help preserve a theater, but “modernization” is sometimes a generous word for erasure. The original stage equipment reveals how productions were mounted; removing all of it would sever that record. I support new safety systems, provided representative old mechanisms remain visible and the alterations are documented. Preservation need not mean freezing a building. It means knowing what changes cost.

Both writers are responding to a proposed renovation. Neither disputes that the existing rigging is unsafe. The debate concerns how to change the theater while retaining what makes its past legible.

Question: Which feature does the director specifically want to retain?

Supported answer: the painted ceiling

Reason: Passage A pairs retaining the painted ceiling with replacing unsafe cables. The supported answer is “the painted ceiling.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.
examples.label: Worked example 2: Two Ways to Keep a Theater

sections.heading: Control the unit, speaker, and condition
body: A detail’s unit is part of the fact. A tool-return count measures tools, not borrowers. Occupied seats at two times do not count distinct visitors over the whole afternoon. A director and a historian can agree about unsafe rigging while disagreeing about retained machinery. examples.text:
A town introduced a Saturday bus between the library and three neighborhoods. Before the pilot, residents at public meetings had asked for daily service. The transport office could initially fund only eight Saturdays. It counted riders and invited anonymous comments after each trip.

The office proposed another eight weeks after the program ended, with an optional fare question on the comment card. The council approved the additional trial without promising a permanent route.

Supported answer: It may have affected demand during the pilot

passage.title: A Translator’s Margins
passage.context:
The translator’s first draft rendered a character’s repeated greeting as “Good morning.” It was smooth English, but the editor noticed that the character used the greeting at night as well. In the source language the phrase had an everyday social meaning that was not limited to time of day.

She reviewed each occurrence, noting who spoke and who answered. Eventually she chose two English expressions depending on the relationship, then added a short note explaining the source phrase’s range.

An early reader complained that the note broke the story’s flow. Another said it helped make sense of a later conversation. The translator trimmed the note but kept it. She did not claim that the new version reproduced every association of the original. Her goal was to preserve the greeting’s work within this particular story, while making the unavoidable tradeoff visible.

passage.title: Measuring a Quiet Street

She wanted visitors to see function and relationship together, without presenting one person’s account as the complete history of every basket. Future labels would include additional voices when available.

lesson.title: Functions
lesson.intro: Function questions reward careful reading more than long calculations. Concentrate on composition order, domain restrictions, inverse branches, and graph features that survive transformations. Every answer should identify an input, an output, or a relationship between them. Label which one the question requests. On digital practice, flag a question when the setup is unclear, keep a short line of scratch work, and return with a definite plan rather than repeatedly trying the same substitution.

sections.heading: 1. Inputs, outputs, and composition
body: A function assigns one output to each permitted input. In f(3), replace every occurrence of the variable by 3, using parentheses if the input is negative or an expression. The notation does not mean that f is a number multiplied by 3. For a piecewise rule, choose the branch using the original input condition before evaluating its formula.

Composition is an ordered process. In f(g(x)), evaluate g first, then feed its output into f. Writing a small input-output chain avoids reversing the order. The two compositions usually differ, and neither is a product of function values. With symbolic input, distribute carefully and square the entire expression.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If f(x) = x² − 4 and g(x) = 3x + 1, then 2 → g → 7 → f → 45. Reversing the chain gives 2 → f → 0 → g → 1. Those two results make an order mistake easy to spot.

sections.tip: Write the inner output on scratch paper before evaluating the outer rule.

sections.heading: 2. Domain restrictions and range endpoints
body: Domain describes permitted inputs; range describes attainable outputs. For real-number questions, a denominator must be nonzero, a square-root radicand must be nonnegative, and a logarithm argument must be strictly positive. These are separate conditions that must all hold. A square root can equal zero, but a logarithm cannot take zero as its argument.

For a composition, also check whether the inner output belongs to the outer domain. For range questions, inspect graph extremes, horizontal asymptotes, and any missing outputs. A downward parabola includes its maximum if the vertex input is allowed. A rational expression may approach an output forever without attaining it.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For f(x) = 1/(x − 3) and g(x) = √(x − 1), the composition needs x ≥ 1 and √(x − 1) ≠ 3. Thus x = 10 is excluded, but x = 1 is allowed. The complete domain is x ≥ 1, x ≠ 10.

sections.tip: Check both the boundary and one ordinary interior value before choosing a domain statement.

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is the real domain of f?
questions.explanation: A real square root needs 12 − 3x ≥ 0, so x ≤ 4. The denominator also requires x + 2 ≠ 0, so x ≠ −2. Both conditions apply at once. The endpoint x = 4 is allowed because the numerator can be zero; a denominator of zero is never allowed.

questions.subject: math
questions.stem: f(x) = 2x + 5 for x < 0, and f(x) = x² − 1 for x ≥ 0.
questions.questionText: What is f(−2)?
questions.explanation: The input −2 is negative, so use the first branch: 2(−2) + 5 = 1. The x² branch would give 3, but that branch does not apply to this input. Select the branch from the input condition before doing any arithmetic.

sections.heading: 3. Transformations without guessing the direction
body: Changes outside a function affect outputs. The rule af(x) + k scales outputs by a and shifts them by k; a negative a also reflects across the horizontal axis. Changes inside a function affect inputs. The rule f(bx + c) reaches an original feature at input h when bx + c = h.

For a parabola in vertex form a(x − h)² + k, the vertex is (h, k), and the sign of a determines whether it is a minimum or maximum. An absolute-value graph uses the input that makes its inside zero. A vertical shift changes the output coordinate, while a horizontal compression changes the input coordinate.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Let f(x) = (x − 3)² + 2 and g(x) = f(2x) − 4. Then g(x) = (2x − 3)² − 2. Setting 2x − 3 = 0 gives vertex (3/2, −2). The horizontal coordinate is divided by 2; the vertical shift subtracts 4.

sections.tip: Solve for the input that triggers the original feature; do not read the inner constant as the shift.

sections.heading: 4. Inverse values and restricted branches
body: An inverse reverses the input-output relationship. The statement f⁻¹(y) = x means f(x) = y. For a single inverse value, solving that one equation is often faster than deriving a full inverse formula. The inverse superscript is different from the reciprocal 1/f(x).

To find a formula, set y equal to the original function, solve for x, and then exchange the variable names. Retain restrictions on the inverse input and output. Squared expressions may give two algebraic candidates; the original domain decides which is valid. To verify an inverse value, substitute the proposed input into the original function.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For f(x) = (x − 2)² + 1 restricted to x ≤ 2, finding f⁻¹(10) gives (x − 2)² = 9. Candidates are −1 and 5, but only −1 lies in the original domain. The correct inverse value is −1.

sections.tip: Circle the domain restriction before choosing a square-root sign.

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is f⁻¹(2)?
questions.explanation: The notation asks for the input whose output is 2. Solve (3x − 2)/(x + 4) = 2: 3x − 2 = 2x + 8, so x = 10. The denominator is nonzero there, and f(10) = 28/14 = 2. The inverse value is not the reciprocal 1/f(2).

questions.subject: math
questions.questionText: What is f⁻¹(18)?
questions.explanation: An inverse value asks which input produces the given output. Solve 5x − 7 = 18, giving 5x = 25 and x = 5. Verify f(5) = 18. The superscript −1 means inverse, not reciprocal or substitution of 18 into the original rule.

reviewQuestions.questionText: Which expression equals f(x + h) − f(x)?

reviewQuestions.subject: math
reviewQuestions.questionText: What is the vertex of the graph of g?

lesson.title: Functions
lesson.intro: Function questions reward careful reading more than long calculations. Concentrate on composition order, domain restrictions, inverse branches, and graph features that survive transformations. Every answer should identify an input, an output, or a relationship between them. Label which one the question requests. On digital practice, flag a question when the setup is unclear, keep a short line of scratch work, and return with a definite plan rather than repeatedly trying the same substitution.

sections.heading: 1. Inputs, outputs, and composition
body: A function assigns one output to each permitted input. In f(3), replace every occurrence of the variable by 3, using parentheses if the input is negative or an expression. The notation does not mean that f is a number multiplied by 3. For a piecewise rule, choose the branch using the original input condition before evaluating its formula.

Composition is an ordered process. In f(g(x)), evaluate g first, then feed its output into f. Writing a small input-output chain avoids reversing the order. The two compositions usually differ, and neither is a product of function values. With symbolic input, distribute carefully and square the entire expression.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If f(x) = x² − 4 and g(x) = 3x + 1, then 2 → g → 7 → f → 45. Reversing the chain gives 2 → f → 0 → g → 1. Those two results make an order mistake easy to spot.

sections.tip: Write the inner output on scratch paper before evaluating the outer rule.

sections.heading: 2. Domain restrictions and range endpoints
body: Domain describes permitted inputs; range describes attainable outputs. For real-number questions, a denominator must be nonzero, a square-root radicand must be nonnegative, and a logarithm argument must be strictly positive. These are separate conditions that must all hold. A square root can equal zero, but a logarithm cannot take zero as its argument.

For a composition, also check whether the inner output belongs to the outer domain. For range questions, inspect graph extremes, horizontal asymptotes, and any missing outputs. A downward parabola includes its maximum if the vertex input is allowed. A rational expression may approach an output forever without attaining it.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For f(x) = 1/(x − 3) and g(x) = √(x − 1), the composition needs x ≥ 1 and √(x − 1) ≠ 3. Thus x = 10 is excluded, but x = 1 is allowed. The complete domain is x ≥ 1, x ≠ 10.

sections.tip: Check both the boundary and one ordinary interior value before choosing a domain statement.

sections.heading: Compare equal intervals
body: Container B cools from 80 to 56 to 40 to 30 to 25°C at 5 min intervals. Its drops are 24, 16, 10, and 5°C.
The temperature decreases throughout, while the decrease becomes slower. A downward graph does not automatically mean a constant rate.

Direction and rate deserve separate descriptions. A decreasing temperature has a negative change, but its rate can become less negative as the water approaches room temperature. In the cooling graph, Container B’s first interval averages −24/5 = −4.8°C/min and its last averages −5/5 = −1°C/min. The water is still cooling at the end, simply more slowly. Never compare vertical changes over unequal horizontal intervals without dividing by interval length. A 7°C decrease over 30 m is steeper than the same decrease over 50 m.

sections.heading: Interpolate between neighboring measurements
body: For Container A at 12.5 min, use 10 min (58°C) and 15 min (50°C). The requested time is halfway, so a straight-line estimate is 54°C.
For the soil mixture at 25% clay, use 20% (18 g retained) and 30% (23 g retained). The midpoint estimate is 20.5 g per 100 g dry soil.

A straight-line estimate uses the fraction of the horizontal interval traversed. At 11 min on A’s cooling curve, the time is one-fifth of the way from 10 to 15 min. Temperature drops by 8°C across that interval, so one-fifth of the drop is 1.6°C and the estimate is 58−1.6 = 56.4°C. A midpoint average works only when the requested horizontal value is halfway. Check whether the problem supplies a specific nonlinear model; if it does, follow that model instead of silently assuming straight segments.

sections.heading: Separate a peak from an unlimited rule
body: The enzyme’s rate rises from 2 at 10°C to 12 µmol/min at 40°C, then falls to 1 at 60°C. “Rate increases with temperature” is only valid over part of the measured range.
A soil pattern measured through 40% clay may motivate a prediction at 60%, but it does not establish that prediction as a measured fact. Extrapolation needs a stated model or cautious language.

A peak is a local feature, not an unlimited guarantee. The highest tested enzyme rate occurs at 40°C, but a fresh trial at 38°C or 42°C could help locate the true maximum more precisely. The data justify “highest among tested temperatures” more directly than “the exact universal optimum.” Similarly, a population that stays at 60 over Days 6–8 has a measured plateau over that interval, not proof that it can never change. Scope words such as tested, estimated, always, and forever often separate a supported answer from an overclaim.
